''Helichrysum bracteatum'' (Vent.) [[Henry Cranke Andrews|Andrews]]
''Helichrysum lucidum'' Henckel{{cite book|author= Henckel v. Donnersmarck, Leo F. V., Graf. |title=Adumbrationes plantarum nonnullarum horti Halensis academici selectarum|language=la|year=1806| page= 5 | oclc=5993095|publisher=Formis F. A. Grunerti, Patr.|location=Halae|hdl=2027/hvd.32044106314206}}
''Helichrysum chrysanthum'' [[Christiaan Hendrik Persoon|Pers.]]{{cite book | last=Persoon | first=Christiaan H. | author-link=Christiaan Hendrik Persoon | title=Synopsis specierum plantarum | volume=2 | page=414 | year=1807 | url=http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/spa/FichaLibro.php?Libro=384 | publisher=Treuttel et Würtz | location=Paris, France | language=la | access-date=26 February 2012 | archive-date=21 February 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120221035440/http://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/spa/FichaLibro.php?Libro=384 | url-status=dead }} }} '''''Xerochrysum bracteatum''''', commonly known as the '''golden everlasting''' or '''strawflower''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]] native to Australia. Described by [[Étienne Pierre Ventenat]] in 1803, it was known as ''Helichrysum bracteatum'' for many years before being transferred to a new genus ''[[Xerochrysum]]'' in 1990. It is an [[annual plant|annual]]{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/184125/Xerochrysum-bracteatum/Details | title = ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 2 August 2021}} up to {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall with green or grey leafy [[foliage]]. Golden yellow or white flower heads are produced from spring to autumn; their distinctive feature is the papery [[bract]]s that resemble petals. The species is widespread, growing in a variety of [[habitat]]s across the country, from rainforest margins to deserts and [[Subalpine zone|subalpine]] areas. The golden everlasting serves as food for various larvae of [[lepidoptera]]ns (butterflies and moths), and adult butterflies, [[hoverfly|hoverflies]], native bees, small beetles, and grasshoppers visit the flower heads. The golden everlasting has proven very adaptable to [[plant cultivation|cultivation]]. It was propagated and developed in Germany in the 1850s, and annual [[cultivar]]s in a host of colour forms from white to bronze to purple flowers became available. Many of these are still sold in mixed seed packs. In Australia, many cultivars are perennial [[shrub]]s, which have become popular garden plants. Sturdier, long-stemmed forms are used commercially in the [[cut flower industry]]. ==Taxonomy== French botanist [[Étienne Pierre Ventenat]] described the golden everlasting as ''[[Xeranthemum]] bracteatum'' in his 1803 work ''Jardin de Malmaison'',{{APNI | name = ''Xeranthemum bracteatum'' Vent. | id = 1543}} Retrieved 21 March 2012. a book commissioned by Napoleon's first wife [[Joséphine de Beauharnais]] to catalogue rare plants that she had collected and grown at the [[Château de Malmaison]].{{cite web|url=http://www.gardenhistorysociety.org/post/publications/book-reviews/jardin-de-la-malmaison-empress-josephine%E2%80%99s-garden/|title=Jardin de la Malmaison: Empress Josephine's Garden|author=Boot, Charles|date=20 January 2010|access-date=22 March 2012|publisher=Garden History Society|location=London, United Kingdom|url-status=usurped|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130203212212/http://www.gardenhistorysociety.org/post/publications/book-reviews/jardin-de-la-malmaison-empress-josephine%E2%80%99s-garden/|archive-date=3 February 2013}} The [[Latin]] species name ''bracteatum'' refers to the papery [[bract]]s (often mistakenly called petals) of the flower heads.{{Cite journal|author=Knight, John|year=1990|title=Golden Everlasting |journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=15|issue=124|pages=335–339}} [[Henry Cranke Andrews]] transferred it to the genus ''Helichrysum'' based on the [[morphology (biology)|morphology]] of its receptacle in 1805,{{APNI | name = ''Helichrysum bracteatum'' (Vent.) Andrews | id = 4318}} Retrieved 21 March 2012. and it was known as ''Helichrysum bracteatum'' for many years. [[Henckel von Donnersmarck|Leo Henckel von Donnersmarck]] described it as ''Helichrysum lucidum'' in 1806, and [[Christiaan Hendrik Persoon]] as ''Helichrysum chrysanthum'' in 1807.{{cite journal|last=Bayer|first=Randall J.|author-link=Randall James Bayer|year=2001|title=''Xerochrysum'' Tzvelev, a Pre-Existing Generic Name for ''Bracteantha'' Anderb. & Haegi (Asteraceae: Gnaphalieae) |journal=Kew Bulletin |volume=56 |issue=4 |pages=1013–1015 |doi=10.2307/4119317|jstor=4119317|bibcode=2001KewBu..56.1013B }} It was given the name ''Bracteantha bracteata'' in 1991,{{APNI | name = ''Bracteantha bracteata'' (Vent.) Anderb. & Haegi nom. superfl.| id = 65989}} Retrieved 21 March 2012. when Arne Anderberg and Laurie Haegi placed the members that are known as strawflowers of the large genus ''[[Helichrysum]]'' into a new genus ''Bracteantha'', and designated ''B. bracteata'' as the [[type species]].{{Cite journal|author=Wilson, Paul G.|year=2002|title=''Xerochrysum'' the correct name for the genus ''Bracteantha''|journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=21|issue=173|page=398}} However, they were unaware that Russian botanist Nikolai Tzvelev had already placed ''X. bracteatum'' in the new, and at the time [[monotypic]], genus ''[[Xerochrysum]]'' the previous year.{{APNI | name = ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' (Vent.) Tzvelev | id = 226129}} This name was derived from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] words {{lang|grc|xeros}} "dry", and {{lang|grc|chrysum}} "golden", likely relating to the nature of the distinctive bracts.{{cite web|url=http://anpsa.org.au/b-bract.html|title=Xerochrysum bracteatum|author=Walters, Brian|date=December 2009|website=ANPSA website|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia)|access-date=26 February 2012|archive-date=25 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225123018/http://anpsa.org.au/b-bract.html|url-status=dead}} Confusion existed for a decade, with ''Bracteantha'' appearing in literature and the horticultural trade until it was clarified in 2002 that the latter name took precedence. Strawflower is the popular name for ''X. bracteatum'' in Europe, while in Australia it is known as an everlasting or paper daisy. An alternate name in 19th-century Europe was ''immortelle''.{{cite book|last=Gardner|first=Charles Austin|author-link=Charles Austin Gardner|title=Wildflowers of Western Australia|edition=17th|year=1990|orig-year=1959|publisher=St George Books|location=Perth, Western Australia|isbn=978-0-86778-007-9|page=144}} ''X. bracteatum'' itself is very variable and may represent several [[cryptic species]]. Alternately, the Tasmanian species ''[[Xerochrysum bicolor]]'' may be combined with it in future [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomic]] revisions.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 57. ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' and its relatives belong to the [[Gnaphalieae]] or paper daisies, a large [[tribe (biology)|tribe]] within the daisy family, [[Asteraceae]]. However, a 2002 [[molecular phylogenetics|molecular]] study of the Gnaphalieae has indicated the genus ''Xerochrysum'' is probably [[polyphyletic]], as the two species sampled, ''X. bracteatum'' and ''[[Xerochrysum viscosum|X. viscosum]]'', were not closely related to each other.{{cite journal|last1=Bayer |first1=Randall J.|author-link1=Randall James Bayer|last2=Greber|first2=David G.|last3=Bagnall|first3=Neil H.|year=2002|title=Phylogeny of Australian Gnaphalieae (Asteraceae) Based on Chloroplast and Nuclear Sequences, the trnL Intron, trnL/trnF Intergenic Spacer, matK, and ETS|journal=Systematic Botany|volume=27|issue=4|pages=801–814|doi=10.1043/0363-6445-27.4.801|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/cpbr/publications/bayer-publications/70.Syst.Bot.27_801-814.pdf|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025}} ''X. bracteatum'' has been recorded [[hybrid (biology)|hybridising]] with ''X. viscosum'' and ''[[Xerochrysum papillosum|X. papillosum]]'' in cultivation, and possibly also ''[[Coronidium elatum]]'' and ''[[Coronidium boormanii|C. boormanii]]''.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 41. ==Description== [[File:Xerochrysum bracteatum head9 - Flickr - Macleay Grass Man.jpg|thumb|left|Wild form showing yellow bracts and orange central disc]] The plant is an erect perennial, or occasionally annual, herb that is simple or rarely branched at its base. It generally reaches {{convert|20|to|80|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in height, but can have a [[Prostrate shrub|prostrate]] habit in exposed areas such as coastal cliffs. The green stems are rough and covered with fine hairs, and are robust compared with those of other members of the genus. The leaves are [[wikt:lanceolate|lanceolate]], [[wikt:elliptical|elliptic]], or [[wikt:oblanceolate|oblanceolate]] in [[leaf shape|shape]] and measure {{convert|1.5|to|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and from {{convert|0.5|to|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. They are also covered with cobwebby hairs. Sitting atop tall stems above the foliage, the flower heads range from {{convert|3|to|7|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter. Occasionally, multiple heads arise from the one stem. Like the flowers of all Asteraceae, they are composed of a central disc which contains a number of tiny individual flowers, known as [[floret]]s; these sit directly on an enlarged part of the stem known as the [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]]. Around the disc is an [[Involucral bract|involucre]] of modified leaves, the bracts, which in ''Xerochrysum'', as in most Gnaphalieae, are petal-like, stiff, and papery. Arranged in rows, these bracts curl over and enclose the florets, shielding them before flowering.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 1. They create the impression of a shiny and yellow corolla around the disc. The intermediate bracts are sometimes white, while the outer ones are paler and often streaked reddish or brown (a greater variety of colours are found in [[cultivar]]s). These bracts are papery and dry, or 'scarious', with a low water content, unlike leaves or flower parts of other plants. They are made up of dead cells, which are unusual in that they have a thin [[Cell wall#Layers|primary]] and a thick [[secondary cell wall]], a feature only found in [[Ground tissue#Sclerenchyma|sclerenchyma]], or structural, cells, not cells of flowers or leaves.{{Cite journal | last1 = Nishikawa | first1 = Kuniko | last2 = Ito | first2 = Hiroaki | last3 = Awano | first3 = Tatsuya| last4 = Hosokawa | first4 = Munetaka | last5 = Yazawa | first5 = Susumu | title = Characteristic Thickened Cell Walls of the Bracts of the 'Eternal Flower' ''Helichrysum bracteatum'' | doi = 10.1093/aob/mcn058 | journal = Annals of Botany | volume = 102 | issue = 1 | pages = 31–37 | year = 2008 | pmid = 18436550| pmc =2712420 }} The individual florets are yellow. Those on the outer regions of the disc are female, while those in the centre are bisexual. Female flowers lack [[stamen]]s and have only a very short, tube-shaped corolla surrounding a [[pistil]] that splits to form two stigmas, while [[Plant sexuality#Individual reproductive unit (a flower in angiosperms)|bisexual or hermaphrodite]] flowers have a longer corolla, and (as in virtually all members of the family) five stamens fused at the anthers, with the pistil emerging from the center. The yellow corolla and pistil are located above an ovary with a single [[ovule]], and surrounded by the [[pappus (flower structure)|pappus]], the highly modified [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] of Asteraceae. It comprises a number of bristles radiating around the florets.Australian Daisy Study Group, pp. 2–3. Yellow in colour, they persist and are thought to aid in the [[wind dispersal]] of the {{convert|0.3|cm|in|abbr=on}} long [[Asteraceae#Fruits and seeds|fruit]].Australian Daisy Study Group, pp. 4, 57. The smooth brown fruit, known as a cypsela, is 2 to 3 mm long with the pappus radiating from one end. In the wild, ''X. bracteatum'' can be distinguished from ''X. bicolor'' in Tasmania by its broader leaves and cobwebby hairs on the stems, and from ''[[Xerochrysum macranthum|X. macranthum]]'' in Western Australia by the flower head colour; the latter species has white flower heads whereas those of ''X. bracteatum'' are golden yellow. ''[[Xerochrysum subundulatum]]'' from [[Alpine climate|alpine]] and [[Subalpine zone|subalpine]] areas of New South Wales, Victoria, and Tasmania is [[rhizome|rhizomatous]], and has markedly pointed orange bracts.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 58. The eastern Australian species ''X. viscosum'' may be distinguished by its rough and sticky leaves.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 65. The plant is a source of [[helenynolic acid]], a rare fatty acid. ==Distribution and habitat== [[File:Xerochrysum bracteatumPB160002.jpg|thumb|''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' near [[Weethalle]]]] ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' occurs in all Australian mainland states and territories, as well as [[Tasmania]].{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Xerochrysum |species=bracteatum||author= Brown, E. A.}}. Retrieved 8 March 2012. Widespread, it is found from [[North Queensland]] across to [[Western Australia]], and in all habitats excluding densely shaded areas. It grows as an annual in patches of red sand in [[Central Australia]],{{Cite journal|author=Nelson, D. J.|year=1974|title=Native Plants in Arid Zone Gardens|journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=7|issue=58|pages=270–279}} responding rapidly to bouts of rainfall to complete its lifecycle.{{Cite journal|author=Maconochie, J. R.|year=1974|title=The Flora of the Australian Arid Zone |journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=7|issue=58|page=255}} It is common among [[granite]] outcrops in southwest Western Australia, and is found on heavier and more fertile soils in the [[Sydney]] region, such as [[basalt]]-, [[shale]]-, or [[limestone|limestone-based]] soils, generally in areas with a high [[water table]]. Associated species in the [[Sydney Basin]] include blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis]]'') in open forest, and the shrubs ''[[Empodisma minus]]'' and ''[[Baloskion australe]]'' in swampy areas.{{cite journal |author1=Benson, Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1994 |title=Ecology of Sydney Plant Species Part 2: Dicotyledon families Asteraceae to Buddlejaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=789–1004 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/97707/Benson_2i.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091004211136/http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0003/97707/Benson_2i.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-10-04 |issn=0727-9620 }} It has been reported growing in disturbed soil, along roadsides and in fields in the [[New England]] region in the United States.{{cite book|author=Haines, Arthur|author2=Farnsworth, Elizabeth|author3=New England Wild Flower Society |name-list-style=amp |title=New England Wild Flower Society's Flora Novae Angliae: A Manual for the Identification of Native and Naturalized Higher Vascular Plants of New England|publisher=Yale University Press|year=2011|page=[https://archive.org/details/newenglandwildfl0000hain/page/447 447]|isbn=978-0-300-17154-9|url=https://archive.org/details/newenglandwildfl0000hain|url-access=registration}} [[File:Xerochrysum bracteatum Everlasting flower from Ooty, India 01.jpg|thumb|Xerochrysum bracteatum Everlasting flower from Ooty, India]] ==Ecology== The brightly coloured bracts act as petals to attract insects such as [[hoverfly|hoverflies]], native bees, and small beetles that pollinate the florets. Grasshoppers also visit the flower heads.{{cite book|last=Elliot|first=Rodger|title=Australian Plants: For Gardens in the Sun|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0uWyUrMIMNYC&pg=PA46|year=2008|publisher=Rosenberg Publishing|location=Kenthurst, New South Wales| isbn=978-1-877058-69-1|page=46}} The caterpillars of ''[[Tebenna micalis]]'' have been recorded on this species, as have those of the Australian painted lady (''[[Vanessa kershawi]]'').{{cite book |title=The Complete Field Guide to Butterflies of Australia |url=https://archive.org/details/The_Complete_Field_Guide_to_Butterflies_of_Australia |last=Braby |first=Michael F.|year=2005 |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |location=Collingwood, Victoria |isbn=978-0-643-09027-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/The_Complete_Field_Guide_to_Butterflies_of_Australia/page/n198 188]}} The tiny fruits are dispersed by wind, and germinate and grow after fire or on [[disturbed ground]]. Flower production is related to increasing day length, and in general, plants produced the most flowers from December to March. Varying planting times or artificially changing light levels might be ways to increase production of flowers outside these months.{{cite journal|author1=Sharman, K. V. |author2=Sedgley, M. |author3=Aspinall, D. |title=Production of the Australian Native Daisies (''Helipterum roseum'' and ''Helichrysum bracteatum'') for the Cut Flower Market|journal=Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture |year=1989|volume=29|issue=3|pages=445–453|doi=10.1071/EA9890445 }} The water mould ([[oomycete]]) ''[[Bremia lactucae]]'' has infected commercial crops in Italy and California. In 2002 on the [[Liguria]]n coast, widespread infection of several cultivars, most severely 'Florabella Pink' and to a lesser extent 'Florabella Gold' and 'Florabella White', resulted in leaf blistering and the development of [[chlorotic]] lesions on the leaves, and white patches on the undersides, particularly in areas of poor ventilation.{{cite journal|author1=Garibaldi, A. |author2=Minuto, A. |author3=Gilardi, G. |author4=Gullino, M. L. |title=First Report of ''Bremia lactucae'' Causing Downy Mildew on ''Helichrysum bracteatum'' in Italy|year=2003|journal=Plant Disease|volume=87|issue=3|page=315|doi=10.1094/PDIS.2003.87.3.315A|pmid=30812773 |bibcode=2003PlDis..87..315G |doi-access=}} There was an outbreak of [[downy mildew]] in a cultivated crop of ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' in [[San Mateo County, California]] in 2006, in which the leaves developed large chlorotic lesions.{{cite journal|author=Koike, S. T. |title=Downy Mildew Caused by ''Bremia lactucae'' on Strawflower (''Helichrysum bracteatum'') in California|year=2007|journal=Plant Disease|volume=91|issue=3|page=326|doi=10.1094/PDIS-91-3-0326A|pmid=30780579|bibcode=2007PlDis..91Q.326K |doi-access=}} A ''[[Phytoplasma]]'' infection damaged ''X. bracteatum'' crops in the Czech Republic between 1994 and 2001, causing poor growth, bronzing of foliage, and malformation of flower heads. Genetically, the [[pathogen]] was indistinguishable from the agent of [[aster yellows]].{{cite journal |author1=Fránová, J. |author2=Přibylová, J. |author3=Šimková, M. |author4=Navrátil, M. |author5=Válová, P. |year=2003 |title=Electron Microscopy and Molecular Characterization of Phytoplasmas Associated with Strawflower Yellows in the Czech Republic |journal=European Journal of Plant Pathology |volume=109 |issue=8 |pages=883–887 |doi=10.1023/A:1026137224558|bibcode=2003EJPP..109..883F |s2cid=23921960 }} The root-knot [[nematode]] (''[[Meloidogyne incognita]]'') attacks and forms [[gall]]s on the roots, which leads to the morbidity or death of the plant. ==Cultivation== [[File:Flower 228.jpg|thumb|right|A European colour form]] ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' had been introduced to [[Plant cultivation|cultivation]] in England by 1791.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. x. German horticulturist Herren Ebritsch obtained material and developed it at his nursery in [[Arnstadt]] near [[Erfurt]] in Germany. He bred and sold cultivars of many colours from bronze to white to purple, which spread across Europe in the 1850s. The bracts of these early forms tended to remain cupped around the flower head rather than flatten out like the native Australian forms. These were also annual rather than perennial forms. Many were given cultivar names such as 'atrococcineum' (dark scarlet flower heads), 'atrosanguineum' (dark blood-red flower heads), 'aureum' (golden yellow flower heads), 'bicolor' (red-tipped yellow flower heads), 'compositum' (large multicoloured flower heads), 'macranthum' (large rose-edged white flower heads), and 'monstrosum' (flower heads with many bracts), although today they are generally sold in mixed seed for growing as annuals.{{Cite book|author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 5|year=1990|pages=267–268|publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=978-0-85091-285-2}} Some coloured forms of South African ''Helichrysum'' are thought to have been introduced to the breeding program, which resulted in the huge array of colours. ''X. bracteatum'' was one of several species that became popular with European royalty and nobility from the early 19th century, yet were little noticed in Australia until the 1860s, when they became more prominent in Australian gardens. [[File:Helichrysum bracteatum 1.JPG|thumb|left|An orange-red-flowered cultivar]] Most of the cultivars brought into cultivation in Australia in the latter part of the 20th century are perennials.Stewart, p. 146. 'Dargan Hill Monarch' was the first of these, and many more have followed. Profusely flowering, these grow in many colours including white, yellow, orange, bronze, pink, and red. Their commercial lifespans are generally around three years.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 60. Queensland-based company Aussie Winners has a range of compact plants ranging from orange to white known as Sundaze.{{Cite web|url=http://www.aussiewinners.com.au/infonotes/Bracteantha_Sundaze.htm |title=Bracteantha Sundaze |access-date=18 September 2010 |website=Aussie Winners |author1=Bunker, Edward |author2=Bunker, Mary |name-list-style=amp |location=Redland Bay, Queensland |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100911090325/http://www.aussiewinners.com.au/infonotes/Bracteantha_Sundaze.htm |archive-date=11 September 2010 }} Plants of this series usually have larger leaves.{{Cite book|title=Australian Plants for Mediterranean Climate Gardens|author=Elliot, Rodger|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TJi4uzF31UQC&pg=PA22|publisher=Rosenberg Publishing|location=Kenthurst, New South Wales|year=2003|page=22|isbn=978-1-877058-18-9}} This range won the ''Gran premio d'oro'' at the Euroflora exposition in Geneva in 2001, for the best new plant series in the previous three years. 'Florabella Gold', a member of the Florabella series, won the award for best new pot plant (vegetative) in the Society of American Florists' competition of 1999. The Wallaby cultivars are range of taller forms with narrow leaves and white, yellow or pink flowers.{{cite book|author=Elliot, Rodger|title=Australian Plants: For Gardens in the Sun|publisher=Rosenberg Publishing|location=Kenthurst, New South Wales|year=2008|page=47|isbn=978-1-877058-69-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0uWyUrMIMNYC&pg=PA47}} Other commercial ranges include the Nullarbor series, and Queensland Federation daisies, including 'Wanetta Sunshine' and 'Golden Nuggets'. ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' is easy to grow both from seeds and from cuttings, although named cultivars only grow true from cuttings. Plants benefit from [[pruning]] of old growth in winter to allow for new growth in spring. Dead-heading, or pruning off old flower heads, promotes the production of more flowers. Fresh seeds germinate in 3 to 20 days and require no special treatment. Plants grow best in [[soil pH|acid]], well-aerated soils of pH 5.5 to 6.3, with low levels of [[phosphorus]]. They are sensitive to [[iron deficiency (plant disorder)|iron deficiency]], which presents as yellowing ([[chlorosis]]) of the youngest leaves while the leaf veins remain green.{{cite journal|title=Foliar Symptomology and Tissue Concentrations of Nutrient-Deficient Vegetative Strawflower Plants|author=Gibson, James L.|author2=Williams, Amy|author3=Whipker, Brian E.|journal=Communications in Soil Science and Plant Analysis|volume=38|issue=17–18|pages=2279–2294|year=2007|doi=10.1080/00103620701588379|bibcode=2007CSSPA..38.2279G |s2cid=96846873|display-authors=etal}} ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' can be grown in large pots or window boxes, and is a good pioneer plant in the garden until other plants become more established. Lower-growing cultivars are suitable for hanging baskets and border plantings. The flowers attract butterflies to the garden.{{cite book |title=Attracting Wildlife to Your Garden |last=Elliot |first=Rodger |year=1994 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne, Victoria |isbn=978-0-85091-628-7 |page=37}} Dried flowers are long lasting—up to some years—and are used in floral arrangements and the cut flower industry. More robust longer stemmed forms are used for commercial [[cut flowers]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/horticulture/floriculture/australian-south-african/accepted#-i-Xerochrysum-bracteatum---i-syn---i-Bracteantha-bracteata--i--(Strawflowers--Paper-daisies)|title=New flower crops now well accepted|year=2005|website=Department of Primary Industries – Agriculture|publisher=New South Wales Government|location=Sydney, Australia|access-date=19 September 2010|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110320103157/http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/horticulture/floriculture/australian-south-african/accepted#-i-Xerochrysum-bracteatum---i-syn---i-Bracteantha-bracteata--i--(Strawflowers--Paper-daisies)|archive-date=20 March 2011}} The main factor limiting lifespan of dried flowers is the wilting of stems, so flowers are sometimes wired into arrangements. Immersing flowers in [[glycerol]] or [[polyethylene glycol]] also lengthens lifespan.Australian Daisy Study Group, pp. 30–31. ===Cultivars=== * 'Bright Bikini' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/184126/i-Xerochrysum-bracteatum-i-Bright-Bikini/Details | title = ''Xerochrysum bracteatum'' 'Bright Bikini' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 30 March 2019}}{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 108 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 10 March 2019}} [[File:Xerochrysum bracteatum 'Dargan Hill Monarch'.jpg|thumb|'Dargan Hill Monarch']] * 'Dargan Hill Monarch' was a natural form collected around {{convert|1.6|km|mi|abbr=on}} inland from [[Cunninghams Gap]] in southern Queensland in May 1961, and registered in February 1977. It is a low perennial shrub {{convert|60|to|80|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} across. The foliage is grey and the large flowers are 7–9 cm in diameter and golden yellow in colour.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc108.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Dargan Hill Monarch'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|location=Canberra, ACT|access-date=17 September 2010}} It grows best in full sun and fair drainage. [[Cutting (plant)|Cuttings]] strike readily, as does seed, although seedlings may differ from the parent. * 'Cockatoo' arose as a spontaneous hybrid between 'Dargan Hill Monarch' and a white-flowered perennial form of ''X. bracteatum'', in the garden of Victorian plantsman Doug McKenzie in [[Ocean Grove, Victoria|Ocean Grove]] near [[Geelong]] in Victoria. He applied to the [[Australian Cultivar Registration Authority]] (ACRA) for registration, which was granted in 1980. It is a dense perennial shrub which reaches around {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and wide. The oblanceolate leaves measure {{convert|6|to|12|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long and are covered with fine hairs that give them a greyish cast. Fine hairs also cover the stems. The flower heads have light lemon-yellow bracts and orange discs and average {{convert|7|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter. They are held on long stems around {{convert|12|–|15|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} above the foliage. Like all forms, it prefers full sun. Although a perennial, it loses vigour after a few years, at which time it is best replaced. The name 'Cockatoo' was chosen as the shape and colour of the ray florets are reminiscent of the wing feathers of the [[sulphur-crested cockatoo]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc189.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Cockatoo'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|location=Canberra, ACT|access-date=18 September 2010}} * 'Golden Bowerbird' is a hybrid, bred by a deliberate [[backcrossing|backcross]] of 'Cockatoo' to 'Dargan Hill Monarch' by Doug McKenzie, who applied for registration with the ACRA in 1980. (It was granted in 1981.) It has much larger flower heads than both parents, yet is a smaller shrub, which reaches {{convert|40|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high by {{convert|70|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} wide. Denser than that of other forms, the foliage is covered in fine grey hair. On stalks around {{convert|10|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} above the foliage, the flower heads measure up to {{convert|9|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter, although larger ones up to 10 cm are occasionally seen. They have around 300 bracts per flower head, compared with 80 for 'Dargan Hill Monarch' and 200 in 'Cockatoo', giving them a "doubled" look.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc226.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Golden Bowerbird'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|location=Canberra, ACT|access-date=18 September 2010}} It is reported as producing fewer flower heads than 'Princess of Wales'.{{Cite journal|author1=Foster, Toney |author2=Kirby, Neil |year=1990|title=Our Favourite Everlastings|journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=15|issue=124|page=343}} * 'Princess of Wales' is a spontaneous hybrid, arising from a cross between 'Dargan Hill Monarch' and an annual form. Arising in the [[Australian National Botanic Gardens]] in [[Canberra]], it was selected by employee Peter Ollerenshaw in summer 1983. He applied to register the cultivar with ACRA in March 1985. It was named in honour of a visit by [[Diana, Princess of Wales]] to the gardens in November 1985, the same month registration was granted. With compact foliage, this form reaches {{convert|60|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and wide. Unlike its parent 'Dargan Hill Monarch', its foliage has hair only on the midrib on the leaf underside. It flowers very profusely, and the large flower heads are borne on stalks {{convert|5|–|9|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} above the foliage. Unlike other forms, the stems wither and die naturally after flowering, making way for more new growth and flowers.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc359.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Princess of Wales'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|location=Canberra, ACT|access-date=23 September 2010}} The flower heads are golden yellow and measure {{convert|6|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} across. * 'Diamond Head' was a natural form collected around Diamond Head in New South Wales, where it is quite common on bluffs and cliffs. [[John Wrigley (botanical collector)|John Wrigley]], curator of the Australian National Botanic Gardens at the time, applied to the ACRA to have it registered, which it was in February 1977. Found on an exposed headland in nature, it grows as a low mat-like perennial shrub {{convert|8|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|60|cm|ft|abbr=on}} across. The foliage is green and rough and the flowers are 3 cm in diameter and yellow in colour with an orange disc.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc107.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Diamond Head'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|location=Canberra, ACT|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=17 September 2010}} It makes an ideal plant for [[rockery|rockeries]], and strikes easily from cuttings during the spring growing period.{{Cite journal|author=Hewett, Max|year=1977|title=''Helichrysum bracteatum'' 'Diamond Head'|journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=9|issue=73|page=205}} [[File:5Everlastings.jpg|thumb|right|Colour forms in cultivation 'Strawburst Yellow', centre, 'Kimberley Sunset' (cream) bottom left, small bronze-flowered form 'Sundaze Dazette Mambo' (far right)]] * 'Hastings Gold' was a natural form from Hastings Point to the east of [[Murwillumbah]] on the New South Wales far north coast. It is a perennial herb with green bushy foliage reaching {{convert|25|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|70|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} wide. The golden yellow flower heads measure {{convert|5|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} across and are held on stalks {{convert|20|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} above the foliage. It is smaller than the similarly coloured 'Dargan Hill Monarch' and larger than 'Diamond Head'.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc159.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Hastings Gold'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|location=Canberra, ACT|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=23 September 2010}} * 'Nullarbor Flame' was a selection introduced into cultivation in 1997 that produces abundant red flowers with yellow discs and a diameter of {{convert|4.5|cm|in|abbr=on}}. The plant grows to {{convert|50|–|70|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} tall and {{convert|50|–|80|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} wide.{{Cite journal|author=Payne, Bill|year=1997|title=New Cultivars now Released for Horticulture|journal=[[Australian Plants]]|volume=19|issue=153|pages=201–202}} * 'Pink Sunrise' was developed by Goldup Nurseries in Victoria in 1986, of unknown origin, presumably a hybrid. It is a compact perennial that reaches {{convert|30|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|60|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} wide. The flower heads are pink in bud, before opening as cream with orange discs.{{Cite web|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc492.html|title=''Xerochrysum'' 'Pink Sunrise'|author=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|location=Canberra, ACT|website=Descriptions of Registered Cultivars, ANBG website|publisher=Australian National Botanic Gardens|access-date=17 September 2010}} * 'White Monarch' was a spontaneous garden hybrid that resembles 'Dargan Hill Monarch' but with white flower heads with orange discs measuring up to {{convert|8|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} in diameter.Stewart, p. 147. * 'Lemon Monarch' resembles 'Cockatoo', but its lemon-coloured flower heads have fewer bracts. It has bushy foliage.{{cite web|url=http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1048829.htm|title=Fact Sheet: Oz Daisies|last=King|first=Melissa|date=20 February 2004|website=ABC Gardening Australia website|publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation|access-date=23 September 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110409073917/http://www.abc.net.au/gardening/stories/s1048829.htm|archive-date=9 April 2011|url-status=dead}} * 'Strawburst Yellow', patented as 'Stabur Yel', is a form with large bright yellow flower heads averaging around {{convert|6.3|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. The result of a planned [[breeding program]] in [[Gilroy, California]], it was bred by Jason Jandrew of Goldsmith Seeds from a lemon yellow-flowered form crossed with a yellow-flowered form in 2005. The pollination occurred in May, the resultant seed was sown in September, and what was to become the [[cloning|clone]] was chosen in December for its large flower size, colour and compact foliage.{{cite web|url=http://www.inspection.gc.ca/english/plaveg/pbrpov/cropreport/stfl/app00006621e.shtml|title=Stabur Yel|website=Canadian Food Inspection Agency website|publisher=Canadian Food Inspection Agency|date=7 September 2010|access-date=25 September 2010|archive-date=5 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120305051647/http://www.inspection.gc.ca/english/plaveg/pbrpov/cropreport/stfl/app00006621e.shtml|url-status=dead}} * 'Lemon Princess' is thought to be a hybrid between ''X. bracteatum'' and ''X. viscosum''.Australian Daisy Study Group, p. 61. ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==Further reading== * {{cite book |title=Everlasting Daisies of Australia|year=2002 |author=Australian Daisy Study Group |author2=Barker, Judy |author3=Greig, Joy |author4=Peate, Natalie |author5=Courtney, Bev |author6=Salkin, Esma |author7=Schaumann, Maureen |author8=Armstrong, John |author9=Thomlinson, Gloria |isbn=978-0-9587439-6-9 |publisher=Shannon Books |location=Melbourne, Victoria}} * {{Cite book |last=Stewart |first=Angus |author-link= Angus Stewart |title=Gardening on the Wild Side |year=2001 |publisher=ABC Books |location=Sydney, New South Wales |isbn=978-0-7333-0791-1}} ==External links== * {{Commons category-inline|Xerochrysum bracteatum}} * [http://anpsa.org.au/b-bract.html ANPSA: ''Xerochrysum bracteatum''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225123018/http://anpsa.org.au/b-bract.html |date=25 February 2012 }} {{Featured article}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q15572857}} [[Category:Flora of New South Wales]] [[Category:Flora of Queensland]] [[Category:Flora of South Australia]] [[Category:Flora of the Northern Territory]] [[Category:Flora of Victoria (state)]] [[Category:Eudicots of Western Australia]] [[Category:Garden plants]] [[Category:Xerochrysum|bracteatum]]
